en: *Commentary on the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*, Scroll Nine, composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhi-zhe.

From the precept concerning the rain-bathing robe up to the precept concerning teaching nuns at will. (The characters in brackets [草書滅法深染傳者須得真] are in cursive script; the meaning is that those who transmit the profound and subtle teachings must obtain the authentic version. This section follows the preceding request.
The Rain-Cloak. The twenty-seventh precept concerning using it before the [proper] time.
These two precepts regarding the rain-cloak are combined into one. The *Po* (Vinaya) says: "Seeking it before the time and using it before the time—both constitute a *pāyattika* offense.
The reason for the regulation—that seeking and using it before the time is not permitted—is that this rain-cloak is an essential necessity for sustaining the body. It is...

Therefore, it was permitted that one might request [the robe] during the designated time. Since the current time has not yet arrived, to request it prematurely and use it beforehand out of a greedy attachment violates the sacred teaching;
thus, this rule was established. The offense is incurred when five conditions are met: first, it is a rain-cloak; second, it is requested before the prescribed time;
third, it is for one's own sake; fourth, the other person gives it; and fifth, one receives and takes possession of it—this constitutes the offense. Question: Regarding "before the time"...

What is the difference between this precept on requesting robes and the precept on begging for robes? The answer is that there are three distinctions: First, the substance of the robe differs. This refers to a rain-cloak (*varṣāśāṭī*), whereas that does not refer to a rain-cloak.

Second, the conditions for permission differ. This allows one to request [a robe] during the proper time; if one requests it outside of that time, it constitutes an offense. That [precept] has no such temporal limit, except for four specific circumstances.

Third, the distinction between relatives and non-relatives: in that case, if the person is a relative, there is no offense; in this case, however, an offense is incurred regardless of whether the person is a relative or not.

The previous [offense] is established by four conditions: first, it is one's own rain-cloak; second, it is obtained during the [proper] season; third, one accepts and maintains it beyond the [prescribed] time limit; fourth, one uses it beyond that limit, at which point an offense is committed.
These two precepts arise from the same circumstances regarding a rain-cloak; therefore, they are formulated together. The *Śāriputrābhidharma* states:
"When seeking [a cloak], it is improper to seek it from various small households here and there for [only] one or two feet. Whether it be for one person or many..."

Seeking from others. Regarding the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there are two parts. From the beginning up to "let it be distributed" (*yāvat samvibhajet*), it clarifies the opening [of the rule] for keeping rain-cloths.

Second, from the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) onwards, it clarifies the faults arising due to the opening [of the rule]. Regarding the former, there are three parts. First, from the beginning up to "desiring the robe," it clarifies the causal conditions for making the vow.
Second, from "The Buddha said to Viśākha" onwards, it clarifies the praise and narration of the eight vows and the permission to receive the rain-cloth. Third, Viśākha...
The passage below explains the eight vows made for the gift of rain-clothing to the Saṃgha. Within the context of the initial causes and conditions for making these vows, there are two parts:
first, from the beginning up to the arrival of the Bhikṣu-saṃgha, it clarifies how Visākhā invited the Buddha for a meal;

second, upon seeing the bhikṣus bathing with their bodies naked, it explains the causes and conditions for her vow to donate rain-clothing. Second, after the meal was finished, she formally made the eight vows. The text says: "She invited the Buddha..."

Regarding making offerings at one’s own residence: the Sūtra states that there are three grades of offerings. Sending food to the monastery is called "superior"; making offerings by going to the residence is called "middling";

building a residence for the purpose of begging for alms and making an offering through the arousal of the aspiration (cittotpāda) is called "inferior. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states: The Buddha said, "Do not encounter people [for the sake of alms]."

The mother of Khā requested, saying, "Grant me my wishes. The Buddha said, "I grant them to you. The fifth [section] says: The mother of Khā asked for nine wishes, yet the Buddha did not grant even one.
These are as follows: "May the World-Honored One always accept my offerings. Regarding the second wish, its meaning is divided into two parts:
the first six wishes arise from internal requisites, while the latter two wishes concern external requisites, namely clothing. This refers to these internal and external [requisites].

Second, regarding the two types of requisites: when one resolves to make an offering, the mind becomes increasingly vast and expansive, entirely free from limitation. One seeks to obtain merit from the "field of the Sangha," which is distinct from ordinary giving;
this is why it is praised by the Buddha. It is truly because of this that [merit] increases. One source states: there are five circumstances for giving that are called "timely":
when someone arrives from afar, when one is ill, during times of famine, when one first obtains new fruits or melons, or if one has newly harvested grain. In these cases, one should give first.
After those who uphold the precepts and are diligent have [received their portions], he then eats himself. The second section has three parts:

first, from "Up to the awakening mind" (*yāvad-bodhicitta*), it clarifies the Buddha’s intention to reciprocate and grant the same vows; it answers the nature of the benefits expected from one's own vows.

Second, from "The World-Honored One" (*bhagavān*) downward, it praises the eight vows as being profound, supreme, and exquisite. Third, from "The World-Honored One" downward, he commands the Sangha to accept them, and thus [the section concludes].

Having heard these words regarding those eight vows, he rejoices that his practice and vows have been brought to fulfillment; thus, he gives rise to a heart of gladness, which is able to eliminate the defilements of stinginess, greed, and the like.

Having abandoned all evils, his body experiences bliss as evil is removed; this is the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*). Through the attainment of ethical discipline, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is gained, which gives rise to sublime wisdom (*prajñā*).

As the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) increase, they are referred to as the "faculties" (*indriya*), "powers" (*bala*), and so forth. Next, in the recitation of the verses, the first recitation concerns the aforementioned eight [vows].

May the causes for these vows be accomplished as profound and supreme. Next, there are two verses that recite the sublime fruits of the aforementioned eight vows. Regarding the first verse, it has two parts:

the first half recites the profundity of the causes of the six vows concerning the acceptance of food; the second half recites the supremacy of the two vows concerning external requisites, namely clothing.
As for "joyful," this refers to the mental state throughout the three periods: prior to the act of giving, during the preparation, and after the gift has been bestowed.

"Purity": because one rejoices in being free from the defilement of stinginess, it is said that the cause of the mind of joyful desire is pure. Although the cause of the mind is pure, if one gives things that are not in accordance with the Dharma, the merit of the gift will likewise be meager.
Next, regarding those who give food and drink: this refers to giving food that accords with the Dharma; thus, one praises the purity of wealth and the purity of the mind.

Wealth is "pure" when the gift is given to a field of merit such as a bhikṣu who maintains the precepts, whereas giving to those outside the fold or to bhikṣus who have broken the precepts is not a superior or clear gift. To maintain [the purity of the gift]...
The Buddha’s disciples immediately praised the purity of the field of merit, noting that since these three factors were all superior, how could it not be exquisite?
Because they offered their robes to the two assemblies, it is called "the multitude. This praises the purity of the material cause.

Although pure giving cannot ultimately sever the fetters, it can temporarily subdue the current mind of greed; hence it says, "subduing the mind of stinginess and envy. This praises the purity of the mind.
The treatise states: "Stinginess (*mātsarya*) is the attachment to and begrudging of wealth; jealousy (*īrṣyā*) is the mind that either endures or cannot endure another's fame, profit, or merit.

It may also refer to a disciple who observes the precepts, praising the aforementioned abandonment of evil as well as faith and joy. "The multitude" refers to the eight types of seeking blessings, such as those traveling afar.
Through the causes of practice, one subdues dog-like pride and greed. One should recite the preceding [verse on] purity. Regarding the words "Who could wish for... the latter two [verses] follow.
Regarding the verse: first, the recipient of the gift completes the fruit; later, the giver of the gift fulfills the fruit.

As for the former, the recipients who have completed the fruit are those such as the deceased bhikṣus who have attained arhatship and so forth—these eight types of persons. Their practice depends upon material support to bring it to completion;
by exerting themselves in their conduct, they will soon realize worldly rewards and ultimately achieve nirvāṇa. It is just as the verse says. These eight matters are for the sake of others.

Regarding "far-reaching" and so forth: Feng says that "basis" (*āśraya*) refers to the internal and external provisions capable of producing happiness for others; thus it is called "the basis of happiness.

As for "receiving the retribution of happiness," this refers to the immediate attainment of worldly rewards as humans or devas, which is termed "receiving the retribution of happiness. As for "permanently attaining peace and security," this refers to the distant attainment of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);

thus it is called "permanently attaining the happiness of peace and security. Regarding "attaining heaven," this explains the attainment of retribution. Regarding "attaining the untainted" (*anāsrava*), this explains the attainment of the lower stages. This is due to practicing giving.

Regarding "attaining the fruit": by relying on the preceding eight practices, one attains human and celestial rebirths in the near term, and the bliss of the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) in the distant term.

Regarding "merit" (*puṇya*): it refers distantly to facing the Sages and generating the cultivation of the eight vows; it refers proximately to the words of faith and joy. This passage cites the causes, followed by the three clarifications of the fruits:

in the distant term, one attains superior progress and the untainted state, whereby one personally adapts the spirit; hence it is called "happiness. This is realized only through personal verification.
It cannot be compared to anything else; hence it is said that nothing surpasses it. By cultivating the causes for rebirth in heaven, one attains long life and constant peace and happiness.

Regarding the third point, relying on aspiration and practice: there was already an aspiration previously, and now one relies upon its practice. If there is aspiration without practice, the aspiration will surely be in vain.
If one practices without aspiration, practice will necessarily be solitary. Because there is aspiration, practice is not solitary; because there is practice, aspiration is not in vain. Zhi says:

"When the person assigned to distribute the rain-clothing is in the midst of the Sangha chanting the distribution of robes—whether they be large or small, four fingers or eight fingers in measure—if there is no one to respond, I shall respond for them.
One who rises to assist in the distribution of remaining robes is also like this. The rest is as before.
One who has entered the rains retreat (*varṣā*) and received a rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭikā*) should be told: "Do not take it elsewhere. The text states:

"If one does not relinquish the rain-cloak and uses it for other purposes," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "This robe may not be used as a formal robe (*tricīvara*). It need not be formally dedicated (*pariṇāmanā*).
One must not wear it while entering rivers, ponds, or lakes to bathe; one must not wear it during light rain; and one must not go naked [while wearing it]."
When bathing the body, one should wear a *śāṭaka* (loincloth) and other old garments; one must not wear various types of formal robes. The ninety-first rain-garment precept states:
"If one has taken emetic or purgative medicine and the head is exposed, it is permissible to eat while in the open air. One may rely on this to construct a screen.
It must always be worn when bathing during heavy rain. If the rain stops early and one is covered in grime and sweat, one may wear it to enter other water."

Washing in the middle incurs no offense. The root text of the precepts consists of four sections: first, the person; second, the request and its limits; third, the establishment of the name and the discernment of the essence;

and fourth, the application of the limits. These are the four sections of the actual root precept. The first is the person. The second clarifies the transgression and the karma; the latter two are easily understood.

The analysis of characteristics and the explanation of the established rules are clearly revealed in the four sections; the wording of the precepts may be understood accordingly. The *Bā* says: "To store rain-clothing."
There are two benefits: first, during the rainy season and the hot season, one may obtain protection for the body while bathing; second, when there is no rain, one may wear the three inner robes.

If there is an intercalary third month, one must request [the robes] on the sixteenth day of the latter third month. If one did not previously know of the intercalary month and requests them on the sixteenth day of the former third month, there is no offense.
If there is an intercalary fourth month, [one must request them] on the sixteenth day of the former fourth month.

The one who observes the *vassa* (rainy-season retreat) may enjoy [the requisites] for up to seven months and a half, or one hundred and twenty days, and may constantly enjoy them throughout this period because the summer is characterized by much rain, dampness, and heat.
If there is an intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*), on the first day of the fourth month one uses [the requisites]. Question:

Within the period of use, why is it permitted to seek [requisites] on the sixteenth day of the fourth month when there is an intercalary month, yet not permitted to seek them during the first three and a half months prior to that?
Answer: Because there is no "totality" (saṃgraha) within the pursuit of greed for the sake of others, the former and latter cases are not the same.

Question: When receiving the *kaṭhina* robe during an intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*), one obtains the merit of using it for many days; should one likewise obtain great profit during an intercalary month? Answer: Clothing provides benefit in many places.

As for opening [the use of] clothing during an intercalary month, there is the fault of increasing greed. Regarding rain-clothing, which is one's own property, there is no excessive increase in greed when its use is permitted during a summer intercalary month.
Therefore, it is frequently said: from the middle of the third month until the end of the third month, one should seek [the materials] and should make [the robes].
If the robe is completed, one may keep it starting from the first day of the fourth month. If the robe is not completed, seeking and making are permitted until the middle of the fourth month.
Even if on the sixteenth day of the third month, it is obtained and completed by the first or second day, the Vinaya masters say that it may also be kept and used; one should examine this.

When the minor regulation (*laghu-saṃvara*) is in effect, one may seek and store [robes] for one month; however, when the major regulation (*mahā-saṃvara*) is in effect, one should seek them for half a month and store them for half a month.
Even if they have not yet been formally accepted (*parigṛhīta*), one must not fail to perform the ritual of purification (*śuddhi*). This refers to the robe accepted for one day.

If one enters the *pūrvavārṣika* (early rains retreat), upon reaching the sixteenth day of the fourth month, one should accept and use it according to the Dharma. Upon reaching the fifteenth day of the seventh month, it should be placed in one location.

One should not keep or use [the robe]; using it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. Furthermore, there is no need to relinquish it. When the time for the coming year’s *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) arrives, one may keep and use it as before;

there is no need to receive it again. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "On the first day of the fourth month, one must formally accept it for one's own use, and shall relinquish it on the fifteenth day of the eighth month.

It is said that because nuns are physically weak and frail, carrying and maintaining it would be difficult; therefore, it was prohibited from being kept. If one obtains [one], [it is as stated above].

One may keep a bathing robe. It is always permissible to wear it, and there is no offense in using it before [the designated time]. One should not seek to obtain one if one already possesses a bathing robe; to do so incurs a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).
Bāyuna says that for the three lower assemblies, keeping one is not permitted, though it is said to be allowed as a general principle. If one discards the rain-cloak, [one may keep this].

This Vinaya does not clarify the procedure for relinquishing [the rain-clothing]. The *Jì* (Mahīśāsaka Vinaya) states in fascicle five: "On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, one should stand before the assembly and make this proclamation:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Now the Saṃgha relinquishes the rain-clothing. This is to be said three times.

If it is relinquished after the sixteenth day, one commits an offense (*vyatikrama*). Thereafter, it may be used for other purposes; it may be made into the three robes, accepted and worn, given to others, or declared pure (*viśuddhi*)," and so forth.
Performing various types of activities, the Vinaya prescribes the method of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*), and there is a textual basis for its acceptance.
This is the twenty-eighth precept concerning the storage of an urgent robe (*āciṇṇaka-cīvara*) beyond the designated time after it has been accepted;

this precept also combines two rules into one. To accept it before the time and store it past the limit constitutes an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). If it is accepted during the proper time but stored past the limit...

Keeping [the robe] also constitutes an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). Both cases arise from the same circumstance of receiving an urgent gift of robes; therefore, they are combined in the regulation.

If it is not an urgent gift, and the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) has not yet concluded, the Buddha did not permit its acceptance. To accept it under such conditions constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (T.1425), fascicle 5, states:

"If the *varṣā* has not yet concluded, to receive a gift for the *varṣā* or to solicit a robe for the *varṣā* constitutes a *vinayātikrama* (transgression of the discipline). This refers here to the summer retreat. Furthermore, this concerns an urgent gift, whether from a relative or a non-relative.

Since both [the donor and the recipient] commit the offense, this differs from the aforementioned case of requesting robes. In contrast to that, this constitutes the offense of possessing an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*). Furthermore, it can be understood that the timing for this differs from the aforementioned case of an extra robe;
as the Buddha established the precept, he did not permit receiving [robes] until the *varṣā* retreat was completed, nor did he permit receiving robes [during that time].
Later, when the minister Li-shi invited monks for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), he offered an urgent donation before the period was complete.

Following the standard rules for the *varṣā*, we were hesitant to accept it, fearing it might contravene the holy teachings. The Buddha, for the benefit of the donor and the advantage of the bhikṣus, permitted its acceptance within ten days.
Because of this sacred dispensation, we accepted the urgent donation after the initial period had passed; however, this violates two teachings and constitutes a transgression.

The realm of greed is deep; it constitutes an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). The treatise states that an offense is established through five conditions: first, it is an urgent gift of robes (*akālacīvara*); second, one knows it is an urgent gift of robes;

third, more than ten days have passed; fourth, there is no valid cause or condition; fifth, upon receiving them, one commits the offense. To store them beyond this period, five conditions must be met: first, they are sufficient as an urgent gift of robes;
second, one knows them to be such; third, they were received within thirty days; fourth, they have not been purified (*pariśuddha*).

There are five limitations; exceeding them constitutes an offense. There are three origins [for these rules]: first, from the beginning until the arrival of the summer robes (*kāṭhina*), when the ship departs, one receives the offering of summer robes.
Second, because the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) requested them prematurely before the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) was concluded, the Blessed One rebuked them and prohibited such practice.
Third, if it is an urgent gift, the World-Honored One permitted its acceptance without fault. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Seven days before the end of the summer."
The Buddha sent Ānanda to bid them farewell, but the people were unwilling to let him go. The Buddha said, "Even if you do not provide offerings, this is the proper custom for guests.
Ānanda went to them and spoke of his distress. Upon hearing this, the brāhmaṇas fainted; they were revived by being sprinkled with water.

Consequently, they brought forth kitchen provisions and followed after the Buddha. Because of this, there are five benefits to the distribution of gruel. [Then] Baddhālī divided the fish. *As he did so...*

The *karmavācanā* and so forth are explained in this precept (*śīla*). Since it has already been permitted to receive [the robe] within ten days, there must also be cases where one receives it more than ten days prior;
however, the text is abbreviated and does not explicitly state this. If one receives it more than ten days prior, it is disconnected from the proper time and the substance of the property is impure;
thus, there is no offense for keeping it beyond that period. This precept has no introductory narrative (*nidāna*), though its explanation exists in the *Śīlavibhaṅga*.

[Commentary: If one receives [the robe] within ten days, it connects with the designated time-period (*kāla*). There is an offense for exceeding that limit. While the *Prātimokṣa* (Precept Text) clarifies the offense for keeping [it] beyond the limit, it does not clarify the offense for keeping it before the limit;

however, such an offense for keeping it before the limit is also possible. In the *Prātimokṣa*, the offense for keeping [it] beyond the limit applies generally to both before and after, as in the case of the half-month bathing precept.
Furthermore, the seven phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* state "exceeding," etc.: first, the person; second, the time; third, the urgent gift of cloth; fourth, the comparison...
The rules established below clarify the karmas; the latter two may be understood. The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states:

"For those who have not completed ten days," this refers to one who receives robes on the sixth day of the seventh month and departs; the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to confess) is held on the sixteenth day, exactly completing ten days.

This is cited to clarify what is not an offense. To resolve subsequent doubts, it is said that "this is an offense" refers to receiving [the robes] within the ten-day period; this constitutes the ten [days].
[The text] says: "The former refers to what was not formally raised; the latter refers to receiving [the robe] within ten days, such that it connects with the designated time.

There is precisely the offense of keeping it after the time has passed. The commentary explains that there is no offense for seeking it before [the time]; once the offense has departed, there is no re-offense. The *Pañcavargika Vinaya-mātṛkā* states:

"Whether during the preceding or subsequent retreat, if ten days have not yet elapsed until the time of the *pravāraṇā*, one may receive an urgently offered robe (*ātyayika-cīvara*). This applies even up to the time when the robes [are normally distributed]."

This constitutes an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. According to this text, even if ten days of the later retreat (*paścima-varṣā*) have not yet elapsed, one may still receive an "urgent gift of robes" (*ātyayika-cīvara*).

The specific characteristics [of this] are omitted here and will not be explained. The second, third, fourth, and fifth passages clarify the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*); the following sections explain the establishment of the rules.

If a bhikṣu [violates] the fifth and seventh of the two clauses below, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. Below, the sixth is explained. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vibhaṅga* states: "Regarding 'urgent gift-clothing' (*ātyayika-cīvara*):
if men or women, whether young or old, whether laypeople or royal consorts, ministers, or those on military expedition;

or if there is a death, a daughter about to be married, or returning home; or at the time of killing bandits, or when a child is ill—if such persons say: 'If not today... (The text here is fragmentary).
If it is gone tomorrow, this is called "urgent robe-giving" (*ātyayika-cīvara*). The text says, "if ten days remain until the *pravāraṇā*. This refers to the *pravāraṇā* on the sixteenth day.
If one receives the robe on the sixth day and departs, and the *pravāraṇā* is on the sixteenth day, there are exactly ten days remaining within the non-seasonal period (*akāla*).
Regarding the passage below stating, "receive the robe on the fifteenth and the *pravāraṇā* tomorrow," this text is excellent and unerring.

Question: Why is it that when receiving robes at an improper time (*akāla*), one may receive them for a period exceeding one month or five months by adding nine days, whereas when receiving them during the proper time (*kāla*), no such addition of days is permitted?
Answer: When robes are received at an improper time, one obtains the allowance for an improper time; however, since this is now being received during the proper time, [the rule does not apply].
How can there be an opening [of the rule] at an improper time? If that were so, then my receiving [the robe] at an improper time would likewise not be permitted during the proper time.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that this must be an urgent gift; since it is received outside of the proper time, one further adds nine days.

As for those who receive it during the proper time, since it is not an urgent gift-cloth, there is no time limit for its reception—why then would it be necessary to further open the rule for nine days? Question: Once the extra robe has entered one's possession, if ten days pass...
Regarding the declaration of purity (*śuddhi*): if ten days have passed, and at the break of dawn on the eleventh day one possesses this *ātyayika-cīvara* (emergency robe), it constitutes an offense.
If it was received on the sixth day of the seventh month, fifteen days have passed; at the break of dawn on the sixteenth day, one should be guilty of an offense.

Why, then, does the text state: "Even if kept for five months, there is no offense"? Answer: This refers to the *atireka-cīvara* (extra robe). Because the time periods are contiguous, there is only the previous allowance [for the first period], and not [the subsequent one].
The subsequent opening occurs ten days later; thus, entering the eleventh day, one commits an offense regarding this "urgent robe" (*ātyayika-cīvara*).

For one who accepts it on the sixth day, until the fifteenth day—before the dawn has appeared—there is no offense due to the prior opening. Upon entering the sixteenth day, it is again a time of subsequent opening.
Because the two openings meet, there is no offense. Regarding those who depart on the fifteenth day: this constitutes breaking the summer retreat and being separated from one's robes.
Since the *vassa* has not yet concluded, leaving the boundary is not permitted; there is only the "subsequent opening," but no "prior opening. To exceed this limit constitutes an offense. Question:
Does the "one-month robe" include the "ten-day robe" so that they together constitute one month? And does the "merit-robe" (*kaṭhina*) include the *kārttika* month so that it constitutes five months?
Why is the *kārttika* month not included among the ten-day robes? And why, after a month or five months have passed, are further days added? Answer:
That a month’s robe includes ten days is due to three reasons for their mutual inclusion: first, the month constitutes a period outside the [regular] season;

second, they share the same functional capacity to prevent the offense of possessing an excess; and third, up to the thirtieth day, it is considered insufficient [for the full allowance], and thus it is permitted.

The month possesses these three meanings; because it is both long and short, it is able to encompass [the other periods]. Regarding the *kaṭhina* robe’s inclusion of the *kārttika* month, it likewise possesses three meanings:
first, the fixed temporal position of one month; second, the equalization of the functional scope for obtaining all five benefits.

The three *kārttika* months are the root; the fifth month is the branch. Because it is insufficient, an exception is granted. Because they are long and short respectively, they are able to include one another.
There are also three reasons why the *kārttika* month does not include the ten-day robe: first, the distinction between the proper time (*kāla*) and the improper time (*akāla*);

second, the difference in the breadth of the benefit; and third, the lack of correspondence between the root and the branch. It is the same for the fifth month not including the ten-day period. *Gāthā*.

It is said: "After the *pravāraṇā*, one who acts as a king of the country may receive a robe offered in haste (*ātyayika-cīvara*). Depending on the number [of days] spent in the rainy-season retreat (*varṣā*), if ten days pass, an offense is incurred.
This first provides a general exemption for the period before and after [the retreat]. Thereafter, a specific exemption is provided;

within this specific exemption, there are first four matters that provide an exemption from the offense of exceeding the period before [the retreat], followed by twenty matters that provide an exemption from the offense of exceeding both the periods before and after [the retreat].
The Twenty-ninth Precept: Regarding the Six-Night Separation from One’s Robes in an Araṇya.
How does this precept differ from the preceding one? There are two points of difference; therefore, it must be further prescribed. First, the previous precept did not apply to an araṇya.

If one stays for even a single night in a village that is peaceful and secure, one commits an offense; however, in a forest hermitage (*araṇya*) that is dangerous, one commits an offense only after staying for six nights.

Regarding these two cases, while the former precept was established because there were no dangers from thieves and the *kaṭhina* robe was available, this present precept was established because of the presence of such dangers.

The receiving of the robe is not accomplished; therefore, there is no exemption. Because there is this specific circumstance, it must be further regulated. The offense is established through six conditions: first, one possesses the three robes;

The robe may be left with a person in the village. Second, the group of six junior monks gave rise to a transgression based on a previous incident. Third, the junior friends rebuked them, leading to the establishment of the precept.

Regarding the group of six bhikṣus: first, they were not people who had long resided in the araṇya; second, they deposited their robes with someone while facing imminent danger. Therefore, the text says:

The original text of the precept consists of ten phrases: 1. When one person is present; 2. The division of time, listing both the proper time and the improper time; 3. The location of the *araṇya*; 4. Suspicion and fear; 5. Clarifying the three robes (*tricīvara*).

Sixth, within the *śayanāsana* (lodgings). Seventh, because it opens [the allowance] for six nights. Eighth, if one exceeds [the limit], the karma is incurred. The final two [cases] may be understood; they are not explained in detail in the *Vibhāṣā*.

Second, the explanation of the remaining nine phrases is clear and may be understood from the text. Question: Why is there no opening [allowance] for the *guṇavat-cīvara* (meritorious robe) in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*?

The *kārttika* month exists by virtue of the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), not by virtue of the acceptance [of the robe]. Therefore, there is the dispensation for the *kārttika*.

As for the text stating "the *kārttika*," it refers to the summer retreat (*varṣā*). It clarifies that the transgression does not belong to this person, because they have received the benefits of the *kārttika*.

Regarding what is called one *krośa*: it is the measurement of the Magadha country; in the north, it is half a *krośa*. In the Middle Kingdom (*madhyadeśa*), the ground is level, and for this reason it is near;

Master Vinayadhara says that this is the definitive meaning. Regarding the fourth point concerning doubt:

In an araṇya (hermitage) or a place of fear, one may suspect of being killed or robbed of one's robes. This fifth point can be understood from among the three robes (*tricīvara*). The *Pañcavargika* states:

When entering a monastery to pay respects, one may not beg for food there. One must not wear [the robes] alone. Regarding those who entrust their two sets of robes to be kept inside the quarters, the *Ji* states:

The *uttarāsaṅga* and the other [two robes] may not be separated from the body. Regarding the seven cases where there is a valid reason for being separated from one’s robe for six nights, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states:

no limit of days is set. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If the preceding or subsequent summer retreat has not yet been completed, and if there is no danger, one must not [leave the robe]."

Regarding the entrusting of robes: In that country, there are many "eighth-month bandits. When the eighth month arrives, they kill people and take their flesh to sacrifice to the gods. On this day, all the people prepare for defense together.
When the bandits arrive on the appointed day and fail to capture anyone [else], they go to the *araṇya* (forest hermitage) and harm the bhikṣus.

Since there is danger, one should not set a time limit for the entrustment. One may receive the entrustment of robes from a layperson (*avadātavasana*), but as for the robes of a householder, since they are not... [the text ends].
While within the boundary, one does not need to go to the forest hermitage (*araṇya*) in sequence; one may assemble the robes without fearing thieves.

Even if it is only the tenth day [of the period], if one goes once to put them on, there may be the faults of dampness, rotting, or being bitten by insects. It is said that if the monastic quarters in the forest hermitage are solid and secure, [this is permissible].

There is no need to send robes; they may not be obtained if they are not secure and firm. Once robes have been sent, after six nights have passed, one goes once to put them on and then returns to the *āraṇyaka* dwelling.

It is often said: "Those who entered the earlier retreat (*pūrvavarṣa*) have already completed it; those who entered the later retreat (*paścimavarṣa*) have not yet reached the fifteenth day of the eighth month.
When the later retreat has just begun and the fifteenth day of the eighth month has not yet passed, it is the sixteenth day of the eighth month, followed by six [nights].
During the night, it is permitted for a forest-dwelling (*araṇyaka*) bhikṣu to sleep apart from his robe. Why is this? Because bandits in foreign lands set out during these six nights;
therefore, this is allowed. Zhi says: "It is permitted for six nights for the sake of stūpas and monastic affairs. For what reason is it permitted for only six nights?
Answer: It was permitted because of specific circumstances. The Buddha sent Upāli to the kingdom of Śrāvastī to settle a dispute regarding the removal of robes.
The robes were heavy, so the Buddha asked, "How many days will it take you to go and return? He replied, "Two days to go and two days to stay. Based on this, a period of six days was permitted.

If the dispute has not been settled within those six days, one may further seek a period of one month; this is also found in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*. However, with the exception of formal monastic procedures (*saṃgha-karman*), once the procedure has been performed, one should act with haste.

Depart quickly. If you receive [an invitation] before a meal, depart after the meal; if you receive it after a meal, depart at moonrise. You must not depart without having settled the matter of the Path (*mārga*).

Except in cases of life-threatening danger or obstacles such as those involving Brahmins, you may depart after settling the matter of the Path. As previously stated, when listing those matters for adjudication, you must not let the time pass.
When returning after the adjudication is concluded, it is as previously stated: you must not wait. While the guest bhikṣus have not yet finished their meal, you must not dye your robes.

Regarding matters such as fumigating the alms bowl, it is not permissible for one who has been invited to stay during the summer retreat to depart midway. The reason for this is that, according to the principles of the Vinaya, one has been invited for the sake of performing specific tasks during the summer;

to travel or stay elsewhere at will would likely result in a violation of the summer retreat. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "In cases involving stūpas, monastic affairs, matters concerning one's preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya), or other personal business, it is permitted to remain for up to six nights.
One may leave behind each of one's robes at a layperson's house; whether it be one, two, or three [robes], [the same applies]."

If one goes on the fifth night and does not return after the business is finished, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). Jīvaka says: "In the case of a *āraṇyaka* (forest hermitage), if one leaves one's robes with a family and stays beyond six nights, it is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).
This interpretation seems plausible; however, since the text regarding other circumstances mentions the absence of fear, we know that the *Liaoshu* (Commentary on the Essentials) states:
"In an *āraṇyaka* location, one must go daily during the summer retreat; staying elsewhere to hear the Dharma is not permitted, and one must always carry [one's robes]."

The three robes must be kept with oneself. If one remains at a residence and fears that they might later be lost, the Buddha permitted them to be deposited elsewhere for up to six nights without loss.
Upon reaching the seventh day, one must retrieve the robes and return; if the seventh night has already passed, they may be deposited again as before.

During the interval while one's affairs are not yet concluded, it is always permitted during the summer retreat (*varṣā*) to be separated from them, provided it is not during the time of the *kāṭhina* robe ceremony, nor during the time when one is formally separated from the robes through a ritual motion (*karmavācanā*).
The Thirtieth Precept: Regarding the Prohibition Against Diverting Property Belonging to the Sangha into One’s Own Possession.

The reason why it is not permitted to divert property belonging to the Sangha into one's own possession is as follows: It is the principle for those who have left the household life to cultivate few desires and contentment.

If one hears that a layperson intends to give to the Sangha, yet employs skillful means to persuade and entice them so that the gift is diverted into one's own possession, this increases internal [defilements].
The fetter of greed causes external distress to the donor and furthermore harms the Saṃgha; this is particularly contrary to what one should practice, and it is for this reason that it is prohibited.
When property permitted for the Saṃgha is confused with one's own personal property, and one diverts it according to one's own whims, joy becomes the cause for its prohibition.

Regarding property permitted for the Buddha or the Dharma, because there is no confusion with personal property and the act of diverting it is difficult to commit, a *pāyattika* is not prescribed. The commission of an offense is established through four conditions: first, it must be property permitted for the Saṃgha.

Regarding the object: first, it is the property of the Saṃgha; second, one forms the perception that it is such; third, having dedicated [the intention]; fourth, as soon as it enters one's hand, the offense is incurred. The root text of the precept consists of sixteen phrases:

first, the person; second, the knowledge; third, the object; fourth, the seeking and entry. The following two points are explained as usual. Regarding the first point, "property of the Saṃgha," the explanation of the third phrase is as follows:

"If a bhikṣu... and so forth, which combines the explanation of the fourth and sixth phrases. There are three kinds of property belonging to the Saṃgha: first, [that which has already been... (Note: The provided fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available text.)

There are three cases regarding property permitted to the Saṃgha: (1) it has been permitted to the Saṃgha; (2) it has not yet been permitted to the Saṃgha; (3) it has already been relinquished to the Saṃgha.

If one diverts these three types of objects toward oneself, the offenses vary in gravity. Regarding the first case, if one diverts the object into one's own possession while perceiving it as permitted, it follows the second case;

diverting the object into one's own possession in this instance constitutes no offense. This is known because, in the subsequent text, it states that perceiving what is not permitted as permitted constitutes a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*); therefore, we know [this].

If it has not been granted [to be returned], yet one encourages [the donor] with the thought that it has not been granted, and the object enters into one's own possession, there is no offense. In the third case, the object has already been relinquished to the Saṃgha;

since this object definitely belongs [to them], if one encourages [the donor] to divert it [elsewhere], one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*). These three cases are all objects belonging to the Saṃgha;

they are explained together in order to clarify the distinctions between light and heavy offenses, as well as the meaning of what constitutes an offense and what does not. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a person brings an object and offers it to a bhikṣu..."
"Where should one give? He replied, "Give it wherever you have respect. He asked, "Where does one obtain the greatest fruit of retribution?

He replied, "By giving to the Saṃgha. He asked, "Who possesses pure ethical discipline? He replied, "The Saṃgha is free from transgressions; [individuals] may not possess pure ethical discipline. If one says, "I have already given to the Saṃgha;
I now give to the Venerable One," there is no fault for the recipient. If one asks, "Where should this object be placed? [the answer is as follows].

[The questioner asks: "If one says, 'I shall always use this as my own property,' how should it be answered? First, the formal conclusion regarding the *thullaccaya* offense is established according to the school’s tenets. Second, if the Sangha grants permission for the object, the following clarifies the favorable outcome (*kṣema*).

There are eight points, arranged in four pairs of distinctions: first, the distinction between the Sangha and the stūpa; second, the distinction between those present and the four quarters; third, the distinction between monks and nuns; fourth, the distinction between those of the same class and those who are not."

This is analogous to the case of mutual exchange. Therefore, it is said that giving to one place and receiving from another is permitted. The *Jìzhù* (祇持) states: "To divert [an offering] toward other individuals constitutes a *pāyattika*;
to divert it toward a larger assembly of monks constitutes a *vinayatikrama*. To divert it toward animals constitutes a *vinayatikrama*.

If a nun diverts a gift intended for one person toward the Sangha, it is a *pāyattika*. The *Jiàn* (見) states: "If one wishes to make an offering to this image, it is auspicious to divert it to that image. The *Shībō* (十波) states: [as above].
There was a sick monk who had companions. The sick monk said, "The Sangha has assigned you to prepare food. I shall eat my portion and give mine to the community as well.
His companions thought, "We have already prepared food for the patient; why should we trouble ourselves to give our own share to the Sangha? They kept the remaining money for themselves.
This is just as in the case of calculating the value. Even unto the Buddha’s words: it is a *duṣkṛta*;

if one has committed a *sthūlātyaya*, or if a donor invites the Saṃgha and, before the turn for food has arrived, says of oneself, "I should know [the time]," this is a *pāyattika* for intentional lying. If it concerns food, one commits a *vinayātikrama* according to its calculated value.

Next is the matter of assigning [an object] for a specific purpose. This is an item that belongs definitively to a particular person. Furthermore, to bypass the proper order and act solely out of one’s own will to harm another constitutes a grave offense.
If, for the sake of a previous person, one preaches the Dharma so as to cause the object to enter one's own possession, one commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

If one diverts property belonging to the *bhikṣuṇī* Saṃgha into one's own use, it is likewise an offense of forfeiture. If property belonging to the *bhikṣu* Saṃgha is diverted to a stūpa, it then becomes the property of that stūpa; there is no need to reclaim it, as it is [meritorious].
Because it is the same [case], the bhikṣu incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. This community is a later community; it is also as described above.

If the property of this *pravāraṇā* community is diverted to that *pravāraṇā* community, the object should be returned to this [original] bhikṣu, who incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. If it is not returned to this community, the value of the money constitutes a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).

If one person from either side diverts it, it likewise constitutes a grave offense. The *Śāriputrābhidharma* says: "A nun solicits offerings for the assembly... even down to [the case of] partial [appropriation]."

The private property of the mind is called "property belonging to the assembly. To divert it toward other groups or relatives constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; to divert property belonging to the Saṃgha constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
It must not be used by the Saṃgha, but should be returned to its original owner. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Manyi lun) is also like this.
