If he sees this woman and does not speak with her, but speaks directly to another woman, and although the first woman hears it, there is no offense.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra* says: When speaking to the later woman, he may move his seat to speak; if the former woman returns and stands within earshot, if he speaks in verse, there is a *pācittiya* for each verse. If...
He spoke in phrases, and with every phrase he brought it forth. If one were to recite a sutra, he would bring forth every detail. Anuṣmṛti said: "Regarding 'a wise man':
this refers to a layman who understands human sentiments and the underlying intent of speech; such a person may serve as a witness. It is necessary that they understand one another's words."
If the categories [of persons] are different, it is not permitted in any case. This applies whether one is a layperson or an ordained monastic; one must not treat them as being the same.
Even if the assembly of monks has gathered, if there are many women and no laypeople present, one must not preach the Dharma for them.

However, one may preach the Dharma to nuns; there is no fault in this, as it serves as instruction for the entire community of nuns. As for "women," they are those capable of receiving sexual intercourse.
If it is a barren woman, a young girl, or one not yet capable of sexual intercourse; if she speaks of worldly affairs, all such cases are auspicious.
Zhi says: "Whether blind or deaf, these are also called 'non-persons. One blind and one deaf—these two count as one. If one is also blind in the eyes, this is also called a 'non-person.

If it is a mother, a sister, or similar relations, it is likewise a transgression. Whether she is under seven years of age or over seven, if she does not understand good and evil [it is a non-person]."
Regarding the meaning and flavor [of the teaching]: he is also called an "ignorant man. If this household is heading toward the road and a bhikṣu is inside, he may preach the Dharma for them.
If passersby on the road do not cease their progress and are able to see or hear it, and if a woman comes to pay her respects and asks the bhikṣu:

"What kind of stūpa is this?"—if one answers by naming the stūpa according to the matter asked about, there is no offense. If a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle requisites) sees or hears [the conversation] but is separated from it, there is no offense;
if both see and hear while being separated from it, it is a *thullaccaya*; if neither sees nor hears while being separated from it, there is no offense.

If a person is performing work and comes toward or away from the interior or exterior, or if they are on an upper or lower gallery and see or hear [the conversation] from afar, there is no offense. If five words are clearly articulated, it constitutes six [syllables] beyond the limit of five.
Sixth: Regarding verbal transgressions. If a woman does not request instruction, one may speak with her at most five or six words. If she requests it, one may speak as much as necessary.
As it is said: "If a woman hears [the teachings], she may answer according to the questions regarding matters from the *Dīrgha Āgama*, even up to the entirety of the Āgamas."
If the sounds are continuous and uninterrupted, it constitutes one *tī* (offense). If they are interrupted, there is a *tī* for every phrase.

If one sentence of the sūtra text and five sentences of the commentary are combined, making six sentences in total, there is no offense. [The factors for this offense are: first, the root text of the precept; second, a woman, distinguished from other objects as a lighter category;

third, exceeding five or six words; fourth, the presence of a man capable of understanding; fifth, the formal determination of the offense. For a detailed analysis of these characteristics, consult the full commentary on the text.
This can be understood. Question: Why is it stated only that "except when invited by a man, there is no offense," rather than saying "except for the invitation"?

Answer: Since it has already been said "except [for a man]," why would it be necessary to repeat "except for the invitation"? If one were to say "except for the invitation," people would assume that even if a man is present, an invitation is still required;

thus, "invitation" serves as a comprehensive term that encompasses the meaning of the invitation. Regarding the five precepts: the precepts themselves constitute the substance (*tattva*), while the ritual of the five precepts manifests their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

The eight precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*) are also like this. The "eightfold fast" (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*) refers to the eight precepts. It is called "closing the gates" because it shuts off the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
If there were not five precepts, one should likewise speak of a "five-gate fast. Answer: Because the gates are not yet complete, it is not given the name "gate.
The eight precepts are the monastic precepts for laypeople for one day and one night. One upholds these eight precepts with purity and detachment, just as the various masters do, closing the gates.
Because it is complete, it is given the name "gate. As it is said in the Sūtra: "It shuts the gates of all evil destinies. Fifth:
whether it be *tsha* or *da*, whether it be explaining the merit of giving, or bestowing the precepts, or answering when a woman asks.
There is no offense in any case.
Regarding the tenth precept on digging the earth, the *Bāyu* states:
"Digging the earth is not permitted. There are three benefits to protecting living seeds: first, to avoid harming sentient beings."

Those who have left the household life to cultivate loving-kindness should take pity on the lives of sentient beings; thus, [the Buddha] established the prohibition against digging [the earth], so as to prevent causing distress and harm.
Second, it is to stop slander. Third, it is to provide great protection for the Buddha-dharma.

If the Buddha had not established these two precepts, all kings would have compelled bhikṣus to perform various types of forced labor; distracted by such worldly affairs, they would have abandoned the cultivation of their proper practice. Because the Buddha established [these rules]...

Therefore, the king calms his mind and no longer subjects them to forced labor, enabling the bhikṣus to cease their worldly involvements and cultivate the Path, so that they may give rise to wisdom, sever delusions, and ultimately achieve the benefit of liberation.
This is called the great protection of the Buddha-dharma. According to the treatise, the offense is established through five conditions; the first is that it is one's native land.

2. Forming the perception that it is cultivated ground (*kṛṣṭa-bhūmi*). 3. Digging it oneself or causing another to dig. 4. When causing another to dig, not using the "pure speech" (*viśuddha-vāk*) of acknowledgment.

5. If [the ground] is damaged, one commits an offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra* states: "There are two kinds of ground: cultivated ground (*jāta-bhūmi*) and uncultivated ground (*ajāta-bhūmi*). As for cultivated ground..."
In lands with much rain, the ground becomes cultivable in the eighth month; in lands with little rain, it becomes cultivable in the fourth month. Excluding these times is called "uncultivable ground.
If one digs at the base of a crumbling wall or a standing stone, or at an anthill mound, for each individual act of digging, there is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

If one digs into cultivable ground, for each individual act, there is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). If one digs into a muddy place until reaching the depth of a knee, or until the entire ground is excavated...

Down to the point of crushing a mustard seed, all such acts constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense (*pāyattika*). However, there is no offense if one draws patterns on the ground for the sake of constructing monastic dwellings, Buddha-stūpas, and the like.

Furthermore, there is no offense in any place where copper or iron is produced, in any mining site, or in places where realgar, stibnite, white plaster, raw stone, black stone, sand, or salt earth occurs; in such locations, none of these are offenses. Pāyu says: "Raw earth" refers to...

The Hu-ben (the original Indic text) says: "Real ground" and "unreal ground": the fourth and eighth months constitute the rainy season, during which the earth remains connected and the moist vapors permeate it, enabling grasses and trees to grow;
this is called "ground where things grow. At other times, when there is no rain, the ground is parched by the sun and the wind blows up the dust;
this is called "ground where things do not grow. If one touches the dry ground above, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense; if one touches the moist ground below, [it is otherwise].
Regarding the offense of falling into a transgression (*pāyattika*): there is no offense if the ground at the base of a wall is level with the damp area, as this is distinct from [ordinary] earth.

Even if the ground has been tamped and leveled, if it is moist and the moisture rises up, one commits a *pāyattika*. Whenever one wishes to take grass, vegetables, or soil, one should speak from a distance, saying, "Bring some clean [material] from such-and-such a place that is good.

If one goes to the edge and points out a specific portion, one commits an offense; (if one sees [the material] and likewise goes to the edge, one commits a *thullaccaya*). An anthill during the rainy season constitutes a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*).
Next, because these are not the fundamental, actual grounds: if grass or trees grow there, touching the grass constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; sealing the earth constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
It is called *duṣkṛta* because it is connected to a minor portion [of the ground]. On the ground beneath mud, one commits a *pāyattika*.

Regarding grass growing on a roof or a wall—such as an anthill mound (*pipīlikā-koṭa*) or a continuous mound (*saṃtata-koṭa*)—or on a covered area of the ground, if earth is raised, one commits a *duṣkṛta*, as does the ground below.

Regarding the offense of *pāyattika* (this passage originates from the regions of Wu and Shu; in the new edition, it is annotated with its provenance because people might find it suspicious or strange). The *Vinaya* states: "In other places, if one sends a messenger to dig the earth by hand, it is auspicious provided the person is not present.

However, according to this present *vinaya*, if one merely instructs another to act while using the formal phrase for "purification" (*jñapti-vākya*), it constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense regardless of whether the person is present or absent.
If one instructs a member of the Great Sangha, even if they say "I know it is pure," it is still an offense.

The Vinaya states: If one rolls stones on the path, leaps and bounds, stamps the ground, runs back and forth desiring to level the earth, or even throws leveling tools that cause damage—even if the injury is as small as a mosquito’s leg—one commits a *thullaccaya* (offense of grave misconduct).
If one employs means to level the ground or sweeps it and causes injury, one commits a *thullaccaya*.
This applies even when dragging wood, driving oxen or horses in and out, or when walking, standing, sitting, or lying down oneself, with the intent [to cause harm].
To cause the ground to become level is also as previously explained. If earth from a riverbank falls because it was trodden down by the feet, one commits a *thullaccaya* offense for every step taken.

If the bank of a pond or ditch collapses while walking or standing nearby, there is no offense. If a clod of earth is too heavy for one person to break, it is a *thullaccaya*; if it is lighter than that weight, there is no offense.
If one throws an object onto the ground without the intentional aim of causing injury, there is no offense. If a bhikkhu in charge of affairs intends to...

Regarding the storage of goods: if they are on bare ground in a living soil, one must have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle such matters) dig them up. If they are in a covered place in dead soil, one may dig them up oneself.

If one drives a stake into the ground, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) for the injury caused, as slight as a mosquito’s leg; when pulling out the stake, there is likewise an offense of *dukkaṭa*.

If one strikes the wall of a room and damages it, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa* if a hole is made that impairs its integrity; if no hole is made, there is no offense. If it is outside and the rain falls upon the ground... [text ends].

If it is damaged, such as having the footprints of mosquitoes or ants, or if characters have been written across the ground, it is likewise permissible to draw upon the unplastered earth without offense.

If it penetrates an old wall, one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle requisites) remove it. If the wall is being demolished, one should have the *kappiya-kāraka* strip away the plaster first, and only afterwards remove it oneself.

If it has not been plastered because it was previously rained upon, one may have the *kappiya-kāraka* remove two or three rows, and thereafter remove it oneself. Upon reaching the foundation, one must again employ a *kappiya-kāraka*.

A person may draw from it. Regarding wells, ponds, streams, pools, and water dripping from eaves: after a fresh rain, one must not draw the water oneself. One should have a *karmadāna* (pure person) draw it;
while the *karmadāna* is drawing it, one should have them stir it for a short time to make it turbid. If oxen or horses have already waded through a pond, one may subsequently draw the water oneself.
Regarding the mud of a pond or the mud of a pool: after a fresh rain, one must not take it oneself. The underlying principle is that rainwater can generate earth.
For this reason, after it has rained, one must not draw water from any ponds or wells by oneself. The *Cīvara-vastu* states:

"When using water for defecation or urination, if one rubs the ground with one's hand, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If rainwater has washed away the main drainage area, one must not take it up by oneself.

If jars, vessels, wood, bricks, tiles, or stones have been left in the open air and have been soaked by rain, one must not take them up by oneself; he who takes them incurs a *pāyattika*. This applies even if they are half-filled with sand."
[The offense of] *vai-dhātika* (transgression). If one digs [earth] oneself many times, it is one *pārājika* offense (*ti*).

If one stops in the middle, it is one *pārājika* for each instance. If one causes another to dig, it is one *pārājika* for every amount dug by that person. If one repeatedly commands "dig quickly," it is a *pārājika* for every such command.
If the earth is already dead, cracked, or rained upon, and one causes a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle things) to take it all away, provided it has been touched by rain.
[Only] after [the ground has been prepared] does one take it for oneself. It is the same with a mouse stealing earth. As it is said: "There is true earth and there is not-true earth.
True earth is that which is free from sand, stones, and rubble; it can be designated as true earth. That which is not true is that which abounds in sand, stones, rubble, and loose soil;
it is called not-true earth. If it is scorched by fire, it is also called not-earth. If the earth contains sand and stones, how [can it be considered earth]?
If one knows that [the ground] can be dug, one should take a small amount of water, mix it with soil, and stir it.
If four parts stone and one part soil can be obtained by digging, it may be dug. If the thickness of the stone is four inches, it may be taken away.

If a wild beast approaches the monastery, for the sake of protecting the dwelling place, a bhikṣu may clear away grass and dig up soil to cut off its path; he commits no offense. However, if he commits an offense such as burning [it] or seizing it with his hands...

[Regarding] "not violating the ground": Pāyuan said, "If one causes a *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) to dig the ground but does not perform the ritual of 'making it pure' (*kappiyakaraṇa*), for every instance [of digging], there is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one instructs a *bhikṣu* or a *bhikṣuṇī*, there is a *sthūlātyaya* offense; if one instructs those of the three lower assemblies, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If those of the three lower assemblies are instructed to act for the benefit of the Triple Gem, they commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Regarding the method for administering medicine: when the Saṃgha obtained a fruit orchard, the Buddha said, 'I allow you to accept it. It was not known who should manage it."
The Buddha said: "Regarding the people of the saṃghārāma, if a śrāmaṇera knows [the source] for this reason, there is no offense for the sake of the Saṃgha.

It is the same for those who cultivate lower-growing plants. Fifth, it is said: there is *araṇya* (wilderness). If a bhikṣu requires earth to make mud, he may take earth from a crumbling bank if a lay attendant (*upāsaka*) is available to supervise;
if none is available, he may take it by sprinkling water on the ground, spreading grass over it, treading upon it to form mud, and then taking it."
To speak in terms of the underlying principle (*artha*): if one is permitted to remove the soil within a house, one should also be permitted to remove the ground beneath that house.
As the text states, "one may remove soil from a collapsed bank," it would likewise follow that one should be permitted to remove the ground from which such a bank has collapsed.
The eleventh precept on destroying living seeds:

The intent behind the formulation of the rule and the conditions for its transgression are entirely the same as those of the preceding precepts. The root text of the precept consists of five phrases: first, a person; second, destruction;

third, a spirit; fourth, a village; and fifth, the offense. Regarding the meaning, "person" and "spirit" are explained as follows. As for the third [phrase], the "village," the fortieth [treatise] states:

Mosquitoes, cicadas, butterflies, and ants—various insects take these as their dwellings. If one cuts, severs, or dismantles them, it constitutes a second offense. There are five types of "villages" (*grāma*);

the following provides a detailed analysis of the fourth type of village distinction. If one perceives living beings where there are living beings, this concludes the fifth section on the determination of the offense.
Now, the fourth phrase is explained: the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states, "One who destroys seeds or breaks a 'ghost-village' commits a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). This refers to root-propagated seeds.
Tea seeds: those that are broken in the middle by force and have their sprouts and eyes removed. Seeds purified by the heart are those such as *rōroku* (coriander) and *ryōran* (indigo).
Seeds purified by rubbing and crushing are the seventeen kinds of grains. Those purified by removing the husk are the five great pure [grains].
Seeds with a shell, such as dates, have their shells removed; they are purified by fire after being peeled and the kernel eaten. Seeds with a covering, such as *hibis* (long pepper)...

Pāṭala: this fire-purifies all food that falls of its own accord when ripe; if it strikes wood or stone below and is injured like the leg of a mosquito, it is called a "wound" (vraṇa), and one purifies it by removing the seed.
Regarding grains that grow with their seeds encased in husks—such as coconuts, walnuts, and pomegranates—one purifies them by fire.
Regarding those whose seeds are wrapped in husks—such as coriander, sesame, and linseed—these have no [visible] seeds; one purifies them by crushing and rubbing, and then by fire.

Regarding "enclosing seeds within the body": this refers to beans, rice, and the like whose seeds have not yet matured; having rubbed and cleaned them until the seeds are thoroughly purified, it is permissible. Māmakī had a granary;
fearing that young bhikṣus who did not know the Dharma would not purify it properly, she had a *karmadāna* (lay attendant) purify it.

Even if they were to go so far as to say "thresh it away" while standing at the edge of the wall, there is no offense. Other similar cases should be understood accordingly. If one throws five raw grains into a pond or a well, [it is likewise permissible].

In the midst [of excrement], in the midst of urine and feces, or having passed through a heap of refuse, death constitutes a *thullaccaya*. If one engages in sexual desire while walking among grass, causing death, it is a *thullaccaya*.

If one injures [an insect] as small as a mosquito's leg, it is a *pācittiya*. The same applies whether standing, sitting, or lying down. One must not remove moss growing on a stone by oneself; one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle such things) do so.

If the sun-dried [food] becomes moldy on its own, one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle food) know of it; once it is known to be moldy from drying in the sun, one may remove it oneself.
If mold grows on cakes, one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* know of it. After rain, when lifting timber or clearing away grass, the *kappiya-kāraka* must lift first;

if a *bhikṣu* assists afterward, there is no offense. When distributing fruit among the Sangha, the *sthavira* (senior monk) asks whether it is pure; if it is not yet pure, he should have it purified.

Regarding "pure": it is said that what is pure may be eaten. While traveling during the summer retreat, fearing one might lose the way, if one gathers rain-affected grass and ties it together as a marker, and later unties it upon returning, there is no offense.
If, on a mountain path, one is about to fall due to mud and rain and the ground is slippery, and one grasps a blade of grass and pulls it until it breaks, there is likewise no offense.

Furthermore, when caught by the current and swept away, one should grasp at grass; as it breaks, one should grasp again (thinking with fear that it might break). One must not use one's hands to push aside water-mosses floating in the water.

If there is a path where oxen or horses travel, one may take [grass] from there; if there is no such path, one should grasp a clod of earth or a stone, throw it upward saying, "Go up to the Brahma Heaven!
If it does not strike [the ground] immediately, the water will part and it may be used (the meaning being that the pure dharma should be thus). Then, one should pick up the ox...

When clearing away excrement, if one cuts living grass, it is an offense of expiation with forfeiture (*pāyattika*). When working with mud, if one is thirsty and wishes to drink water, and has mud on one's hands, one may drink from within a leaf.
If there is no attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*) to fetch water, one may go to a tree and drink from within its leaves; one must not pull the branch to break it off.

If the height is unattainable, one may shake the tree to cause the leaves to fall. One may drink from dry, fallen leaves. If the leaves have already withered and turned yellow, cutting them constitutes an offense of transgression (*dukkaṭa*). This applies even when flowers are present.

If [a lotus root] is half-ripe, it is a *vyatikrama* (transgression); if fully ripe, there is no offense. If one turns over water-lilies (*piṅgā*) in the water, it is a *vyatikrama*; if one throws them onto the bank, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).

When entering the water to wash, if aquatic plants stick to one, one should pour water on them to cause them to enter the water. If one cuts morning fungi (*pratyagra-tṛṇa*), it is a *vyatikrama*. Thus says the Commentary.

If one requires flowers or fruit, one may grasp the branch; however, one must have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to make things permissible) take them down, or likewise have the *kappiya-kāraka* pull them down.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: regarding the planting of various grasses and trees, if there is something required, one should say to the *kappiya-kāraka*, "You know this. If he does not understand, [one should explain].
He speaks again, saying, "You must wear this. If [the other] does not understand, he speaks again, saying, "I need this.

If [the other] still does not understand, he says, "Give it to me. This is likewise a violation of the earth. If there is living grass covering the path, and one ties it up on one side to block the view, or if branches are broken to clear a path, or if leaves fall unintentionally, there is no offense.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra* states: "If one covers living grass or vegetables with seven layers of grass for the purpose of killing them, it is a *pāyattika*."

If one eats fruit by swallowing the seeds, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). If one tells a lay attendant (*upāsaka*) to shake a tree so that fruit falls, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).

If one places seeds in hot water, or dries them in the sun or roasts them with fire, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one takes floating duckweed from the water, or takes *śilavai* (stone-reed), it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The *Gāthā* says: "To strike ripe fruit. [The Buddha] replied: "One may bend the tree through supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), or blow upon it with the wind."
If seeds die; if one kills grasses and trees by throwing wood at them; if they are submerged in water, burned by fire, or pounded in a mortar;

or if one covers growing grass with ash, soil, sand, or other such means—it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. If one says to another, "Take these fruits, I wish to eat them," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one takes them oneself, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. Master Dharmaśreṣṭhin said: "It is not permissible to eat any fruit that contains seeds."

One may eat at all times; there is no need for a knife. One eats after cleaning with the fingernails. The Buddha himself stated that regarding raw fruits and vegetables, it does not matter whether they have seeds or are seedless;

they must be purified by fire before eating. Regarding unclean fruits containing seeds: swallowing them whole is *pācittiya* (an offense requiring expiation), while chewing them apart is *dukkaṭa* (an offense of wrong-doing).
Now, to further explain the fourth point: although raw seeds are fivefold in meaning, when divided, there are three types. The first type is...
There are three types of birth: birth from roots, birth from branches, and birth from seeds. Within birth from roots, there are two divisions.

That which does not depend on a node for growth is termed a root-seed (*mūlabīja*). That which depends on a node for growth is termed a joint-seed (*kandabīja*). Among branches, there are likewise two:

that which does not depend on a node for growth is a branch-seed (*skandhabīja*), while that which depends on a node for growth is designated as node-born (*parvaja*). Regarding seed-seeds (*bījabīja*)... [the text continues].
The substance is established as one; from its initial state to its final differentiation, it forms five [categories].
The commentary states: *haridrā* is translated as "yellow ginger. Thus, in the present Vinaya texts, both the foreign (Sanskrit) and Chinese names are made manifest.
*uśīra* is translated into Chinese as "coriander. *hatacchada* is translated into Chinese as "sparrow-head. *kālānusāri* is yellow *utpala* (iris). *turuṣka* is unknown.
Furthermore, it may be known that *śamā* means the Bodhi tree, and *rāvaṇa-udumbara* means the tree possessing many fruits.
These two kinds of trees exist in Jiaozhou but are not seen in other regions. The *sumanā* flower resembles the *mallikā* flower; it exists in Guangzhou. Its vines grow there.
As for *rāvaṇa* and *puṣkara*, these are all unknown [to me]. If one perceives the thought of arising toward what is arising, then one descends and descends, and attains liberation.

The fifth section concerns the determination of offenses, which is divided into two parts. First, it clarifies that for the five types of living seeds, regardless of their specific kind, if one destroys them while they are on the ground or detached from the ground, the offense is a *pāyattika*.

Second, regarding plants and trees of the seven colors, it clarifies that for those not among the five types of living seeds, if one destroys them while they are on the ground, the offense is a *pāyattika*.

If one destroys auspicious objects off the ground, this Vinaya prescribes that a single act may destroy multiple types [of objects]. Whether the destruction is slight or great, the formal offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) is incurred as for a single act of killing many beings;

it is likewise incurred according to the number of objects involved. Question: Why is it that when driving a stake into a tree, one incurs a separate offense for each blow regardless of whether the blows are many or few?

Furthermore, since animals are destroyed according to their respective parts, why is there no *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) for each part destroyed? Explanation: Grasses and trees possess... [text ends]
In most cases, wherever life is destroyed, it obstructs another portion such that birth cannot arise; therefore, these are classified as "killing according to destruction.
As for animals, they possess only a nominal life-force; thus, it must wait until death occurs before it is termed "taking life," and consequently, only one offense is incurred.

Furthermore, the prohibitions differ because the intent behind the regulations varies in gravity. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one simultaneously destroys five types of seeds, one simultaneously commits five *pāyattika* offenses;

each *pāyattika* offense is burned away [by confession]. Whether acting oneself, or by writing, or by dispatching a messenger, or by indicating signs—in all such cases of instruction, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: 'If one simultaneously destroys five types of living seeds, there is one *pāyattika* offense according to the karma.'"

The offenses are not determined by the object. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika*, whether one acts oneself or instructs another, the offense is likewise determined by the karma, as explained in the preceding precepts.
The twelfth precept concerning "harassing the Saṃgha with discordant speech":

Generally, the karma of body and speech is subtle and difficult to restrain; although a transgression may not reach the level of gravity, the act of harassing the assembly is no small matter and must be addressed.

The monastic community performed a formal act of censure (*karmavācanā*), yet he did not desist. He continued to violate the Dharma and disturb the Sangha; the transgression incurred was no small matter.

According to the treatise, this offense is established through five conditions: first, the karma of body and speech is frivolous; second, he acts repeatedly and does not cease; third, the community performs a *jñapti* (a formal motion) to censure him.

When the Saṃgha issues a formal summons according to the Dharma, if one violates it five times, one commits an offense. Prior to the establishment of the precept, the bodily and vocal karma involved constitutes frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*);

since there was as yet no monastic command, the communal law could be contravened, and one would incur only a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*). After the precept is established, to violate it constitutes a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

Regarding "frivolous speech": this is a term for speaking in a discordant manner; "frivolous bodily action" is a designation for causing provocation and vexation. Although these two offenses are distinct in their sequence, they are identical in their nature of contravention.

Because it is a single prohibition, they are combined and not divided. The commentary states: Although these may be true words, because they are spoken at an improper time, they are called frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*).

Alternatively, even if spoken at a proper time, if they accord with decline and affliction and lack benefit, or even if they are beneficial, if the words lack a foundation, the logic is disordered, and they are spoken with a defiled mind, all are termed frivolous speech. Question: What about the other three verbal transgressions? They are direct [faults].

If one acts, one commits the offense immediately; why does this not depend on a formal monastic decree? The answer is: regarding the other three types of karma, first, they are directly contrary [to the precepts], and second, the gravity of the harm and affliction is significant;

therefore, one commits the offense immediately. This frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*), however, is the opposite of these two principles; thus, by merely engaging in it, one commits a light offense.

Furthermore, it is more serious than a formal motion (*jñapti*). Thus, the gravity of the offenses differs. Question: Regarding this precept, one has not yet committed an offense after the formal motion is completed; rather, one commits the offense by acting again.

As for all precepts concerning admonition, one commits the offense immediately upon the completion of the admonition. Answer: This constitutes an act that disturbs the Saṃgha and is not the proper method of admonition.

It is appropriate that the Saṃgha establish a regulation through a formal motion. Until one violates the Saṃgha’s regulation, there is no offense. Only when one acts again after the regulation has been established does it constitute a violation of the regulation; the offense is then formally determined based on that subsequent action. This is consistent with [the principle of]...
The admonitions differ. Zhi says: "When he heard Dhāna call, he did not come; when not called, he came. He sat or did not sit; he spoke or did not speak.

It was known that his not going was likewise so. There was no violation of the formal announcement (jñapti), yet because he caused the eightfold affliction of the Saṃgha, the precept was subsequently established."

If a bhikṣu treats another with contempt, it is a *thullaccaya*. If he dismisses many people, or even his preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or the community of monks (*saṃgha*), by sending them away or refusing to go [when summoned], it is an offense of transgression (*vinayātikrama*).
If someone asks, "From where have you come? and he answers, "I have come from the past"; or asks, "Where are you going?
and he answers, "I am going to the future"; or asks, "Where do you sleep? and he answers, "On eight pieces of wood"—if he answers incorrectly in such ways, it is an offense of transgression.

[If] one answers differently when questioned within the Saṃgha, it is a *pāyattika*. Likewise, if one speaks falsely before the assembly, or before many people, or before an upādhyāya, an ācārya, or an elder, it is a *pāyattika*.
When asked about things such as fingernails by a thief who has arrived, one may remain silent without committing an offense, provided one fears that it would lead to a schism in the Saṃgha.
If one knows or suspects [the truth], yet says "I do not know" when one does know, this constitutes "speaking otherwise."

Answer: In each case, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense separately. Question: In the section on "bodily frivolity" (*kāyavikṣepa*), it says, "Having finished the formal motion (*jñapti*), he speaks thus.

Since it refers to "bodily frivolity," why does it mention "speech"? Answer: Speech fundamentally expresses the body; now, having summoned someone and they do not come, they violate the Sangha and cause distress.

The meaning is the same as that of the words. It is often said: if one was a *śrāmaṇera* who returned to lay life after breaking the precepts, and later becomes a *bhikṣu*, or if one’s gender changes and becomes a *bhikṣuṇī*, such cases involve the original *karmavācanā*. All *karmas* may be performed together;

one may receive other scriptures and may also receive scriptures from others. However, one must not act as an *upādhyāya*, provide formal reliance (*niśraya*), or keep a *śrāmaṇera*. If one asks about other matters...
The Dharma-affairs shall not fall into ruin; it is auspicious for those who engage in question and answer. If one confesses the offense committed, one obtains the *karmavācanā* of release.
The four clauses of the Prātimokṣa:
The thirteenth precept concerning disparaging and reviling the administrative officials of the Saṃgha.
All monastic affairs are difficult; their administration is not easy. Therefore, one should select those who have cultivated virtue to manage them according to the Dharma, which is worthy of praise.
Yet, instead of encouraging them to work diligently, one may respond with malice and anger, speaking words of resentment and abuse that cause the other to suffer distress.

This leads to the neglect of monastic affairs, a harm that is not slight. Regarding the offense, it is established through six conditions: first, being appointed by *karmavācanā* to oversee monastic affairs.
1. It is a person. 2. One knows that this is an appointment by the Saṃgha. 3. One manages the affairs according to the Dharma, free from attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion.
4. One speaks words that may be disparaging or abusive. 5. One’s speech is clear and distinct. 6. The person addressed hears and understands; or they hear but do not see, or they see but do not hear.
One then commits an offense. Question: What is the difference between this precept and the previous precept regarding verbal abuse? Answer: There are four differences.

First, the previous precept concerned one who was not a monastic administrator (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*), whereas this concerns a monastic administrator. Second, the previous precept did not distinguish between truth and falsehood, whereas here, speaking the truth does not constitute an offense.

Third, the abusive words differ. Fourth, in the previous case, if one was not an administrator, the offense was light when there was mutual absence of seeing or hearing; here, because of the respect and protection [due to an administrator], the offense is heavy even if there is mutual absence of seeing or hearing.

The *Pārājika* offense is excluded because, as one who is not an administrator (*vaiyāpṛtyakara*), I have no involvement in the matter; yet you have arbitrarily brought up past events, whether true or false, and thus commit an offense.

The two preceding precepts are identical in that they both involve harassing the Saṃgha; since the status of the administrator is not distinct from the subject here, they are combined into a single precept.

The root text consists of three phrases, which can be understood through the detailed explanation of their characteristics provided below. The fifth [section] states: "If the Saṃgha performs a *jñapti*, a *jñapti-dvitīya*, or a *jñapti-caturtha* [karma], they shall appoint an administrator..."

Regarding those who serve others: if one falsely accuses them of being driven by desire, hatred, fear, or delusion, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong speech) for every such statement, even if the person was not appointed by the Saṃgha through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) or if they were someone other than the appointed official.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vibhaṅga* states: If the Saṃgha performs a ritual according to the Dharma and appoints fourteen persons to admonish those who harbor suspicions, then for one who speaks with malice, it is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

If the ritual is abandoned, it is a *duṣkṛta* for twelve persons and a *thullaccaya* for two persons. These two [positions] are: first, the instructor of nuns; second, the one who delights in the mountains.

Regarding the *dhātu* (realm/element): "one who eats people. These two persons undergo the *karmavācanā* of renunciation (*pratyākhyāna-karmavācanā*). As for the lower *karmavācanā* of renunciation, all incur a *sthūlātyaya*. The *Gā* says:
"If one transmits to another what was said in malice, it is all *duṣkṛta*. The *Ji* says: "The person who performs the prostration is the officially appointed person.

The person who prostrates to the *zhú* (a type of official) is someone hired by him to prostrate to the *zhú*. 'Now' refers to the debtor; he further hires another person to perform the censure. All three persons incur a *sthūlātyaya*."

It is said that there was once a great fish with one hundred heads, each of which was different. This was because [the fish] had previously committed the offense of harsh speech as a Tripiṭaka Bhikṣu.
When excellent food was being distributed among the assembly, if a full ladle were given to the senior monk (upādhyāya), the senior monk should say:
"Are all the others being treated this way? If he replies, "I am giving it specifically to the senior monk," he should say: "There is no need; distribute the excellent food equally to everyone."
When receiving food, the senior monk (upādhyāya) must not accept it immediately; he should say, "Give it equally.

If a novice (śrāmaṇera) or a lay attendant (karmadāna) gives more to his teacher or a venerable elder, the administrator (vaiyāvṛtyakara) should say, "Give it equally. The other person replies, "Why do you not do it yourself?
The administrator then pushes that person aside and orders another to do it. The administrator says, "In the food of the Sangha, there is no distinction of high or low; you must give it equally."

Regarding "giving equally" and then "reproaching": if one takes one's own food and sits beside another, eating from their bowl while saying, "This is equal," this is called "reproaching" but not "giving equally.
Thus, there are four permutations: two are *vinayātikrama* (transgressions of discipline), one is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation), and one is without offense.
The Fourteenth Precept on Spreading Monastic Bedding:

In general, monastic property is of great value and should be cherished and protected. Furthermore, because one might harbor exclusive attachment to it, failing to examine its condition leads to negligence.

Therefore, the *Bhikṣu-vinaya* states that this rule was established for three reasons. Regarding the method for handling monastic bedding: first, all property belonging to the Saṃgha from the four directions must be treated with utmost care.
First, regarding the offerings bestowed by faithful donors, the benefits derived from their use by the Sangha are vast;

it is therefore appropriate to protect them so that they may support the practitioner’s body and conduct, thereby enabling the attainment of peace and happiness. Second, since these are the property of the donors, one should cherish them with a careful mind, ensuring they are always available for use.

This causes long-term faith and respect; thus, the three applications are completed. By immediately setting aside [the bedding] so that it does not damage the property of the Saṃgha, the merit of its use is instead channeled back to benefit the donor, thereby bringing their roots of goodness to fulfillment.
For these three benefits, the Noble One established this rule. Regarding the offense, it is constituted by six conditions:

first, it must be a bedding item belonging to the Saṃgha of the four directions; second, one must know it is the property of the Saṃgha; third, it must be in an open space; fourth, one must have spread it oneself.

One causes another to spread [the bedding]. Five: when departing, one does not lift it oneself, nor does one instruct another to lift it. Six: one commits an offense as soon as one leaves the door. Regarding the origin of these rules, there are two parts:
first, from the beginning up to the point of impurity, clarifying the transgressions arising from usage; second, the prohibition of the monks' food without censure.
The root text of the precept has four phrases: first, a monk; second, property belonging to the Saṃgha; third, on bare ground; fourth, clarifying that it is for the sake of...
Having already spread out bedding for the Saṃgha and used it in an open space, one incurs the offense of *pāyattika* for failing to store it away upon departing.

This is explained below; the first point may be understood as stated. Regarding the second point concerning *saṃghika* property, there are three parts. First: if one fails to store away *saṃghika* property, one incurs a *pāyattika*. Second:
if the property has not yet been relinquished to the Saṃgha, there is no *pāyattika* for failing to store it away. Third: when the property has already been [relinquished]...
The Sangha has offered a gift, yet it has not yet been given to the Sangha; if it is spread out, it will bring good fortune.

If a bhikṣu, after having unfastened the third tier from beneath a monastic rope-bed and departed, and if there is an old resident who unfastens the fourth tier but does not put it away, therein are three points:
from the beginning until the preparatory act of coming and going, one intends to unfasten it but does not put it away; first, one must reverse the unfastening and put it away.

Method. Second, if a bhikṣu [fails to act], the following clarifies the non-performance. As explained above, such an instance constitutes an offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) once the person has exited the door.
Fifth, it says: There was a bhikṣu who saw monastic bedding (*śayanāsana*) lying in the open air; he neither spread it himself nor had anyone else spread it.

If one does not lift up bedding after sitting or lying upon it, it is a *thullaccaya* (offense of grave misconduct). The Buddha said: "It is likewise a *thullaccaya*. If one goes to a nunnery and spreads out bedding for the nuns but does not lift it up, it is also a *thullaccaya*.
If a layperson enters the monastery, they should borrow monastic bedding for their use. If there is a gathering at a layperson's house...
One should borrow bedding and requisites. If a bhikṣu eats and does not put away [the items], it is also a *thullaccaya*.
If the person in charge of affairs exposes the Sangha’s bedding in the sun, and one sits nearby in meditation or falls asleep, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Cīvaravastu* states:

"If an image is placed upon a Sangha bed and a bhikṣu, while prostrating, touches it with his hand and does not put it away, it is a *pāyattika*. If many people are prostrating and all touch it with their hands, the responsibility belongs to the last person."
There is no offense if one leaves [the bedding] for twenty-five moments after having spread it out during the spring months and entrusted it to someone.

If there is a person lying upon it, one must entrust it to them immediately. If a bhikṣu rises at night to relieve himself and touches the Sangha’s bed, and having touched it once, departs, he commits a *thullaccaya* for each instance of touching and departing.
If an administrator wishes to entrust the bed and bedding, he should take them outside and place them in an open space; if he leaves them there and departs... [omitted].

Twenty-five cubits [is the distance for] the *tiṭṭha* (standing) practice. If one has received a monk’s bed or mat and, after exposing it to the sun, departs while leaving it twenty-five cubits away, one incurs a very grave offense.
During the rainy season, this is not sufficient; therefore, one must wear heavy robes during the rains.

Thus, if while traveling on a road one sits upon uprooted grass, when departing one should gather it up before going. It is said: "If one undertakes the superior *dhūta* practices, or if one is under a tree..."
If one is in an open space, one must not even take up the *kāṣāya* or stay under a roof.
One may use the monastic bedding (*saṃgha-śayanāsana*) outdoors, provided that one can protect it; even the *kāṣāya* may be used if it is covered so as not to get wet.

For those who observe the middle dhūta practice, there is no [prohibition against staying] in the open air during the rainy season; during the rainy season, they may use the monastic bedding under a roof. This applies likewise to beds.
Having spread out a mat on the open ground, if one does not intend to return immediately, one must go beyond the distance at which a person can throw a stone;
if one goes beyond that, it is a *pācittiya*. If one goes beyond the distance at which two stones can be thrown, it is a *thullaccaya*. It is said:

"If one has spread out a mat on the open ground and departs for a distance exceeding forty-nine paces, it is a *pācittiya*. One must not wander about without having entrusted one's belongings to someone else.
*Pāyantika*: The fifteenth precept concerning the spreading of monastic bedding in a private place.

The intent for its inclusion is the same as before. Regarding the analysis of the offense, it is established through six conditions: first, it must be monastic property; second, one must know it to be monastic property; third, [it must be spread in a private place...]

[The first four cases concern] secluded places. Fifth, not putting away [the object] when departing; sixth, the offense is incurred upon exceeding the limit. The reason they are separated [into two categories] is:

first, the distinction between secluded and exposed places; second, the difference in the time the offense is incurred. In an exposed place, one incurs the offense upon leaving the door; in a secluded place, one incurs the offense upon crossing the boundary.
If one resolves to depart permanently and does not return to cross the boundary, it constitutes an offense. If one intends to return and crosses the boundary, there is no offense.

It is permitted to stay outside the boundary for two nights; if one exceeds three nights, it constitutes an offense. There are three distinct conditions for exemption: in the case of exposure to rain, one may stay for two nights in a sheltered place during times of urgency. Question:
Regarding the aforementioned misappropriation of the Sangha’s property and the aforementioned mutual use by nuns, as well as this present precept, each lists three types [of offenses].

Regarding the property of the Saṃgha: what is the distinction between its various types? Answer: Among the aforementioned cases of misappropriating Saṃgha property, this refers specifically to taking permitted items, as well as mutual exchange, which involves taking [property] and subsequently relinquishing it to the Saṃgha.
Since both are indeed the property of the Saṃgha, these three types are listed; one must distinguish their differences. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"If entrusted to an administrator or to an individual who is virtuous, meritorious, and observant of the precepts—there is no one like such a person."
Entrust this to virtuous and wise persons and those who guard the monastery; do not entrust it to those who are shameless and violate the precepts, even if they are as young as novice monks.

It is often said: If a visiting or resident monk leaves the boundary with the intention of returning, should an urgent cause arise such that he cannot return by the appointed time, he is free from fault.
However, if he leaves the boundary without intending to return and fails to do so by the appointed time, it constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense.
The Sixteenth Precept: Regarding the Prohibition Against Forcibly Spreading Bedding to Annoy Others.

Generally, material things are limited and their use is restricted; when the sentiments of both parties are equal, one must consider whether the other intends to occupy the space or has already done so.

Thus, one must deliberate on whether it is appropriate to proceed. Nevertheless, knowing that another has already obtained a dwelling place, one nonetheless deliberates and then forcibly spreads bedding within it.

To mutually press and revile one another is not the decorum of those who have left the household life; therefore, this rule was established. According to the treatise, an offense is established through five conditions:

first, having previously borrowed a dwelling place and already settled therein; second, knowing that others were already residing there; third, intending to disturb and annoy them; fourth, forcibly spreading out bedding within it;
and fifth, incurring the offense according to whether one sits or lies down. Of the five phrases in the root precept, the third concerns "forcible spreading," and the fourth...

To cause disturbance to another’s mind constitutes five offenses of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. In the detailed explanation of their characteristics below, the second is omitted; the remaining four may be understood by consulting the text.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If, for the purpose of annoying another, one opens a door or makes a sound, or extinguishes a fire or lights a lamp [to disturb them]."

If one performs chanting, recitation of vows, reading scriptures, or preaching the Dharma [for personal gain], it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense for each instance of acting contrary to the wishes of others.
Regarding the seventeenth precept on forcibly ejecting another from a monastery cell:

although monasteries belonging to the Sangha of the four directions are intended for communal use and should not, by principle, be restricted to individuals, even if one has previously prepared and settled someone there...

This is the *Śamatha* [concentration]. Those who come later should enjoy it together. To harbor anger within and forcibly drag another out—both ruining oneself and distressing others—is the root of contention;
the harm caused is not slight. The offense is established through four conditions: first, it is a dwelling for the Saṃgha of the four directions during spring or winter;

second, one has previously settled there in meditative concentration; third, one acts with the intent to disturb and annoy that person; fourth, one drags them out of the room. This is the root of the precept.
There are four points: first, the person; second, internal anger; third, that it is not an offense if the monk’s quarters are clearly demarcated as private;

fourth, the formal offense is incurred by dragging another out of the quarters. In the detailed explanation of the characteristics below, the second point is briefly left unexplained. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When dragging another bhikṣu..."
If he drags the pillar, seizes the door, or leans against the wall, and one thus pulls him away from each respective spot, it is an offense of *thullaccaya* for each place.

If he scolds verbally, it is an offense of *pācittiya* for each word according to the monk’s speech, and for each place. If he uses skillful means to drive him out, it is also an offense of *pācittiya*.

If he drives him out of the *ārāma*, it is an offense of *dukkaṭa*. If he angrily drives out snakes or rats, it is an offense of *dukkaṭa*. If he says, "These are useless things," and drives them out, there is no offense. (10)

Kātyāyanīputra said: "If one sleeps with a snoring sound while feeling joyful, one should rise and perform walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). If one cannot perform walking meditation, one should go to a secluded place. One must not disturb others.
Sending a messenger, using hand gestures, or driving someone out from a private room; throwing another’s robes or bowl;

or pulling them out to an open space—all such acts constitute *duṣkṛta* (offenses). Maudgalyāyana said: "If one pulls someone out by hand oneself, from the bed down to the ground, and dust falls [from the movement], up to the point where they reach the ground."

Even if he causes the five groups of monastics or laypeople to pull [the object], the bhikṣu incurs a *thullaccaya*. If he causes a bhikṣu to pull it, both incur a *pācittiya*. For the four lower groups of monastics, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

If he causes those who are deaf, blind, sightless, mentally deficient, or mute to pull it, they incur a *saṃghādisesa* offense. A śrāmaṇera who is practicing the *chārattamānatta* (six-night penance) also incurs a *pācittiya*.
One who has committed one of the thirteen *antarāyika-dhammas* incurs a *dukkaṭa*. If he sends a bhikṣu into a bhikṣuṇī’s dwelling, it is a *pācittiya*. If a bhikṣuṇī does so privately...
It is auspicious [to do so] within a room. As for the five cases mentioned: if one drags someone from a rear room to a front room; or if one drags them from a front room out onto the porch;
or if one drags them from the porch into the courtyard; or if one drags them from the courtyard out into the outer area—in all these instances, it is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

If one brings an unpleasant person with the intent to make them leave of their own accord, it is a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) whether they leave or not. If it is for the purpose of disciplining a disciple, however, dragging them out is permissible.

There is no offense. To pull someone down [from their seat] before the fourfold assembly incurs a *duṣkṛta*. Question: The previous precept permitted [the use of] property belonging to relatives and friends without distinguishing between those who are pure and those who are impure;

why is this [present case] restricted to those who are pure, yet does not exclude relatives and friends? Answer: The former case involved objects belonging to laypeople that had been previously lent to another;

since there was no compulsion from the relative or friend, it was permitted. Furthermore, as it was not a dwelling place of the Saṃgha, purity was not distinguished. This present case concerns a Saṃgha room; for one who is pure, there is communal residence.
Meaning: Regarding "impurity," there is no sense of communal residence; one may expel [the offender] without offense. The Eighteenth Precept:
Sitting on a Bed with Detachable Legs on an Upper Story.

In all matters, one must be circumspect regarding danger. One must exercise great care regarding houses that have thin roofs and beds with detachable legs; one must not cast oneself down to sit upon them.

Lying down. There may be a risk of falling and injuring those below; since the resulting distress is not slight, the Noble One’s regulation is necessary. Regarding the offense, it is established through four conditions:
first, it is a multi-storied building; second, the covering is thin; third, the bed has removable legs; fourth, one sits or lies down with the body relaxed—this constitutes an offense.
The four phrases of the root precept are: first, a person; second, a multi-storied building; third, a bed with removable legs; fourth, the act of sitting or lying down.
Regarding the offense: this is fully explained in the section on defining the characteristics [of the rules]. The *Jì* (Śikṣāsamuccaya) states:

"As for a bed with legs, if the tips of the legs point upward when entering a house, it is as if one leg-tip has been discarded while the other three are round; even if all four leg-tips are pointed, one must lift it. If all four legs are round, there is no offense provided there is no one beneath it.
Only according to this principle does this single leg count as detached; if two or three are likewise detached, it should be understood in the same way. The *Gā* [Vinayavibhaṅga]... [text continues].
It is said: "Except for monasteries belonging to bhikṣus, it is auspicious to sit or lie down in the monasteries of the other four assemblies or in the monasteries of non-Buddhists.
The Nineteenth Precept on Using Water with Insects to Mix with Mud:

Generally speaking, compassionately saving the lives of sentient beings is the essential core of the Way. To knowingly consume water that contains insects while intentionally making use of it is particularly harmful to living beings.
[The Buddha] commanded: "To violate the path of compassion and merely exist for one's own sake is irrational; such a matter is not trivial. Therefore, this rule is established.
The offense is completed through four conditions: first, there is water containing insects; second, one knows it is water containing insects; third, one does not employ the method of straining;

fourth, one uses the water as received, at which point the offense is incurred. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Whether the insects are large or small, if there are still insects after three layers of straining bags, one must create [a finer filter] again."

If, upon careful inspection, one still perceives insects, one should abandon that dwelling place and depart. If one uses water containing insects, for every single application of water, there is one *pāyattika* offense;
for every inhalation or exhalation, according to the number of breaths, there is an offense. If one causes another person to apply the water, there is one *pāyattika* offense for every word spoken.

If one causes a sick person to apply it, there is a *pāyattika* offense for every word spoken. The birth of insects is impermanent; they may have been previously absent and now exist, or they may currently exist and later cease to be. This is so.
Therefore, one should examine it carefully every day; if there are no insects, one may then use it. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

There were certain generals who, having been converted by a nun, were dispatched by the king to go on a military expedition. When their bowstrings were exhausted, they took water-strainers with them, thinking that if they encountered water containing insects, they should strain it before drinking.
The king asked them in great anger, "You have deceived me! If you would not even drink water because of tiny insects, how can you possibly kill enemies? The generals replied, "The insects..."
Those who have transgressions shall be disciplined; this will cause no harm to the state, and for this reason they are strained. The King was greatly pleased.

At that time, when the generals arrived at the battlefield, some attained the *maitrī-citta-samādhi*. Because they entered the power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), the bandits were immediately subdued.
The *Dharmaguptaka* says: "Regarding this precept against taking life, there are four rules of training (*śikṣāpada*); this was the first to be established. Since it is not permitted..."
He used water containing insects to mix with grass, soil, and mud, and then drank it. Since he was prohibited from drinking [water with living beings], he then stopped taking the lives of animals.
Since he could no longer take the lives of animals, he then stopped killing humans. Because the circumstances were distinct, four separate precepts were established;
all are designated as "first" [offenses]. If one wishes to prepare a dwelling place, one must first use a fine cloth, one cubit in size, to filter the water.

When it is covered, the room is completed and may be used. Once three sections have passed, the offense is finalized; the room is no longer usable.

With palms joined in reverence, regarding the teaching of the Dharma: whether it be Abhidharma or Vinaya—wherein the ninefold Sūtras are called Abhidharma, and the detailed and abbreviated versions of the Prātimokṣa are called Vinaya—one must instruct the nuns. When a nun arrives, one must not lower one's head;
rather, one should stand with proper deportment. If one sees her with hair oiled and smoothed, or dressed in fine, dyed garments, or wearing clothes that have been pounded [to soften them]...
Make it glossy. Tie a white sash around the waist. To one who is thus prepared, one should speak, as previously described.

When a bhikṣu who is a relative is giving instructions, if there is a layperson present in front, one must not speak, lest that person give rise to unwholesome thoughts, thinking, "He is instructing me according to his own whims.
If the wife does not speak, then later on, that teacher-monk may conceive the notion that she is a woman, and the nun [conceives the notion] regarding the teacher...
As for the perception of a Buddha, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one goes to the nuns' residence to provide instruction, one should say to them, 'Lay out seats;
I shall go. If one is able to go, one should sweep and sprinkle the place of residence as previously described."

Next, the second section is explained: the analysis of the three phrases regarding the offense of failing to appoint [a formal instructor]. First, the right and wrong of the day of instruction, as already explained in the *Jìzhù* (Commentary on the Vinaya).

Second, regarding the quantity of offenses incurred, there are four phrases. Under the two phrases concerning "failing to appoint," first, if one goes without being appointed by the Saṃgha, it is improper;
one incurs two offenses because they constitute a single course of action (*ekakarmasamutthāna*), and the offense is completed on the first day, while the second day is improper.

It is like the case of building a house: although both [offenses] are transgressions, there is only one offense because they arise from the same causal conditions. Thus, regarding the eight rules of respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*), it is taught that by committing them together, one incurs one *thullaccaya*.
The second case is when one goes on a day other than the designated day; this is not a single *thullaccaya*, as explained above in the two phrases concerning the appointment by the Saṃgha.

In the first instance, going on a day other than the designated day, there is only a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) and no *thullaccaya*. In the second instance, being appointed and going on the designated day, neither of the two offenses exists.

Third, regarding the explanation of the text: It is said that if a monk who has not been appointed by the Saṃgha recites the Eight Respectful Rules (Aṣṭau Gurudharmāḥ), it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

This is because the text of the rules is fixed and the transgression is minor; thus, it results in a *duṣkṛta*. If he preaches the Dharma in a casual manner, it is difficult to distinguish between the correct and the false, as there is the possibility that he might preach false doctrine, thereby destroying the mental conduct (*citta-carita*) of the nuns.

Because this transgression is grave, it constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense. On days other than those for preaching the Dharma or the Eight Respectful Rules, one likewise incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense, because on such days, preaching is not permitted.
Regarding the instructions: "Not on the day" constitutes four offenses—three *duṣkṛta* and one *sthūlātyaya*. "Going on that day" constitutes two offenses—one *sthūlātyaya* and one *duṣkṛta*.
Now, the failure to assign the day is not the same as the eight *gurudharma* rules; it is combined with the *duṣkṛta* because their names are identical.

In the subsequent section on preaching the Dharma, only the failure to assign the day is mentioned without explicitly citing the "not on the day" rule, because the offense for preaching the Dharma is more serious, whereas the "not on the day" rule [is less so].

Because it is a minor offense (*laghu*), the specific day is not cited, but rather the failure to observe the proper timing is penalized. Now, regarding the explanation of the eight points of respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) for preaching the Dharma:
there is no distinction between light and heavy offenses. Second, because they are called "equal obstructions," both the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* state:

"If one enters a nunnery without having informed a virtuous bhikṣu to instruct and preach the Dharma to a nun who is not ill, it is a *pāyattika*. However, the subsequent text in both sources provides exemptions; there is no offense for a nun who is ill. Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
When two bhikṣus are staying in a secluded place, if one of them wishes to enter a bhikṣuṇī monastery to provide instruction, he must inform the second person.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vibhaṅga*: "If one who has not been appointed by the Saṃgha provides instruction to bhikṣuṇīs—whether for one, two, three, or four bhikṣuṇīs—one incurs as many *thullaccaya* offenses as there are individuals instructed, according to what is permitted.
If there is only one bhikṣu present, the bhikṣuṇīs should go to him and request instruction; this applies whether there are two or three [bhikṣus].

It is thus. To explain that the day is not the proper time for preaching the Eight Respectful Precepts (aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ), one incurs two offenses, as has already been clarified in the preceding text.

As the text states: "Alternatively, if one preaches the Eight Respectful Precepts on a day that is not the designated day of instruction, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. This refers to the fact that the day is not the proper time;

the reason no offense of "not being dispatched" (*an-avasarjana*) is incurred is that this has already been concluded within my own *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*. Furthermore, the phrasing may vary to mutually illustrate the point; here, the focus is placed on the Eight Respectful Precepts to conclude the argument.
[Date] is incorrect. This refers to the offense of instructing [a nun] without being appointed. There are two types of cases where one is not appointed:

either one simply instructs on the Dharma without mentioning the Eight Respectful Rules, or one directly instructs on the Eight Respectful Rules; in both instances, one incurs one *thullaccaya* (grave offense). If both are taught, one incurs a single offense because they constitute a single act.
Therefore, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "The offense of instructing without being appointed. Here, "not appointed" refers to the instruction on the Dharma.
Question: Regarding this precept, if one assigns [a monk] or does not assign him on the day [of the assembly], and both fail to provide instruction, one commits a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense);

yet for the subsequent precept, whether one assigns him or not, if one speaks until sunset, one should likewise commit a *pācittiya*. Answer: When the Saṃgha has assigned someone to preach the Dharma and it reaches sunset, it is governed by the rules of the community (*saṃghadharma*).
Because the nuns do not dare to leave, one commits a *pācittiya*. However, if one speaks without having been assigned, there is no involvement with the rules of the community.

Regarding the taking of a nun under one's care: if the nun departs, there is no offense; the fault lies entirely with me. Therefore, it is a minor offense, specifically a *pāyattika* (提), because it does not include the gravity [of other offenses].

It is given a distinct name. As for those appointed by the Saṃgha during the non-observance of the day [of rest], the offense of failing to appoint is grave, while the offense itself is light, being merely a *duṣkṛta* (吉羅).

Because it applies to both light and grave cases, they are collectively designated by a single name. Although there is a gradation in principle, the cases for both parties are similar; thus, in the end, there is [this distinction].

What harm is there? Regarding the *bhikṣuṇī*’s *duṣkṛta* offense: this is not a minor offense for failing to instruct the *bhikṣusaṃgha*. Rather, it is the offense of unilaterally requesting an instructor (*śāstṛ*) without having been appointed by the *bhikṣuṇīs*.

As for the two lower assemblies [the *śrāmaṇerī*s and *śikṣamāṇā*s], they do not receive appointment from the senior *bhikṣuṇīs* when going to the *bhikṣusaṃgha* to perform prostrations and participate in the communal recitation (*poṣadha*).
The same rule applies to the *śrāmaṇeras*.
